scenes.heading: Generics: Type Parameters
scenes.narration: Let's explore generics, added in Go 1.18, which let you write functions and types parameterized by a type instead of copy-pasting per type.

scenes.heading: The core idea
items: Type parameters go in square brackets: [T any]
A constraint is an interface limiting allowed types
scenes.narration: A generic function declares type parameters in square brackets before its ordinary parameters. Each parameter is bounded by a constraint — an interface that says what the type must support. The result is one implementation that works for many concrete types, without copy-pasting per type and without losing the compile-time safety you would give up by falling back to the empty interface.

scenes.heading: From generic definition to call
steps: Compiler checks operations against the constraint
Infer the type argument from ordinary args
scenes.narration: When you call a generic function, the compiler usually infers the type argument from the ordinary arguments, so call sites stay as clean as regular calls. It then instantiates the definition for that concrete type and type-checks the result. The constraint tells the compiler which operations are legal on the type parameter — so comparable permits equals, and an ordered constraint permits the less-than operator.

scenes.heading: A type-safe generic Map
scenes.narration: Here Map takes two type parameters, T and U, both constrained by any. It converts a slice of T into a slice of U by applying the function f to each element. At the call site we pass a slice of ints and strconv.Itoa, and the compiler infers that T is int and U is string — no explicit type arguments needed. One definition now works safely for any input and output types.

scenes.text: Go keeps full type info — it uses GC-shape stenciling and dictionaries, not blanket erasure to interface{}.
scenes.narration: A common misconception is that generics are just the empty interface under the hood. They are not. Go keeps full type information and type-checks each instantiation, implementing generics with a mix of compile-time stenciling by GC shape and hidden runtime dictionaries. That avoids the boxing and type assertions an interface-based approach would pay.

scenes.text: Use generics where they clearly remove duplication — slice helpers, Min/Max, type-safe containers.
scenes.narration: Generics remove the old trade-off between reuse and type safety. Reach for them where they clearly cut duplication, like slice helpers, numeric Min and Max, or type-safe containers, but resist over-abstracting — idiomatic Go uses them surgically, not everywhere.
